teaching_card.title: Sequences and Series (Hard)
teaching_card.body: An arithmetic sequence adds the same difference d each step: a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same ratio r: a_n = a₁·r^(n−1). A recursive rule tells you how to get each term from the ones before it.
key_points: Arithmetic: a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d; sum of n terms = n(a₁ + a_n)/2.
Geometric: a_n = a₁·r^(n−1); find r by dividing consecutive terms.
Use n − 1 steps from the first term, not n.
Recursive rules: compute term by term from the starting values.

screens.title: Arithmetic sequences
screens.body: Subtract consecutive terms to find d. The nth term is the first term plus n − 1 jumps of d. Given two far-apart terms, divide their difference by the number of steps between them to recover d, then work back to a₁. The sum of the first n terms is n times the average of the first and last terms.

screens.title: Geometric sequences
screens.body: Divide a term by the previous one to find r (it may be a fraction or negative). The nth term is a₁ times r raised to n − 1. The sum of the first n terms is a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). Two known terms give r from the ratio r^(gap) = later ÷ earlier.

screens.title: Recursive rules
screens.body: A recursive definition such as a₁ = 3, a_n = 2a_(n−1) + 1 tells you to build each term from the previous one: 3, 7, 15, 31, …. Write the terms out in order and stop at the index asked for. To identify a rule from a list, test whether consecutive terms differ by a constant (add) or divide to a constant (multiply).
key_points: Compute recursive terms one at a time.
Constant difference → add; constant ratio → multiply.
Check the rule against the first three terms.
